prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: After the full round-1 exchange my configuration is unchanged: a single B007 part naming Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The scientific case is the one all six of us accept: proglucagon processing and the insulinotropic action of GLP-1(7-36) amide, the identification and synthesis of the active peptide, receptor and tissue biology, then independently replicated outcome trials in diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular and renal disease. Maturity is not in question. The chair asks that the principle be stated before the name is chosen, so I state mine: the prize rewards the discoveries that established what the hormone is and what it does, and the citation may name the therapy as the consequence but should not credit it as the achievement. On that principle Holst and Drucker are fixed, and the third place belongs to the person tied to the identity of the active form. The citation is worded narrowly, as 'identification of its active form', so that it claims no more than the credited names can support and does not rule on who else contributed.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is still Knudsen's absence. Acylation-based half-life extension turned a peptide with a half-life of minutes into a once-daily and once-weekly drug, and Sandberg is right that this took real scientific insight. A prize that names the physiology and not the analogue design can look like it skips the step that reached patients. Mojsov's priority is disputed, Habener is not on the supplied list, and I cannot settle the dispute from the supplied record. My position therefore rests on a judgement about the principle, not on evidence that her priority is secure, and I accept that the committee could reasonably decide the other way if it chooses to honour development explicitly.

responses.point: Sandberg argues that Knudsen's acylation design is a scientific contribution in its own right, decisive for the outcome trials, and that dropping Mojsov on contested priority could be read as ratifying one side. He said he would accept the Mojsov trio if the committee decides on a discovery-level prize.
responses.response: I accept the correction to my round-1 wording: acylation and albumin binding are scientific work, not routine engineering, and I no longer describe them as merely development. We now differ only on the principle, which is where the real choice lies. I keep the discovery-level reading because Knudsen's design builds on the identification and action of the active peptide, which Holst, Drucker and Mojsov established, whereas the reverse is not true. Your concession that the Mojsov trio is the more defensible choice under a physiology prize is the position I am asking the committee to adopt. I agree that leaving her out would settle a contested question without evidence, and this is why I will not move on a statement of doubt alone.

responses.point: The chair holds Knudsen on the ground that the Medicine prize has repeatedly honoured the step that makes a discovery usable, that acylation is original, and that he cannot verify Mojsov's credit from the supplied text. He would move if peptide identification were judged more decisive.
responses.response: Your difficulty with verification is fair and I share it, since I cannot verify the priority either. But the same limit cuts both ways: if the supplied record cannot show Mojsov's priority to be weak, then excluding her is as unverified as including her, and the burden should not fall only on her. Past prizes that honoured usable therapies mostly did so where the credited work was also the discovery, as with the physiology here. I would therefore answer your question this way: peptide identification is decisive for what the active hormone is, and a citation worded narrowly around it is supported by the names. I do not claim this settles it and I respect that you may weigh translation more heavily.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius argues that dropping Mojsov only settles the uncertainty against her without evidence, and that the citation should name the physiology so that the prize stays anchored in what was found. She also ranks B004 below B041 on impact, not on scientific quality.
responses.response: I agree with her reasoning on B007 and on keeping the citation anchored in physiology, and I have taken her emphasis on supportability into my wording. On B004 I accept that its disease consequences are developing while CAR-T already shows durable remissions, and I do not claim that B004 outranks B041 on impact. My order between them rests on attribution: Walter's Ire1 kinase-RNase mechanism and Mori's transcriptional response are complementary and decisive, and her point that Ron and Kaufman are not in the supplied credit means that this cleanliness depends on the list. So I treat the two alternatives as close, with B004 first only if the B041 originator problem cannot be resolved within three names.

responses.point: Perlmann keeps the basic-discovery trio, says contested priority is a reason for care and not for exclusion, and would move to B004 first, ahead of B041, if B007 stalls on attribution.
responses.response: I agree with the principle and with his willingness to be shown evidence that Mojsov's contribution is subordinate. Neither of us has that evidence, so the discipline is a narrow citation, as he proposed. Where I would add a point to his: if the committee decides the principle is development, I would not stall B007 over it. I would accept Knudsen in third place as a legitimate outcome over leaving the prize unresolved, because the shared judgement that B007 comes first is much stronger than my confidence in the third name. I would move to B004 only if the credit in B007 were shown to be unworkable, not because the third name is contested.

responses.point: Linnarsson prefers Mojsov on the ground that identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) form is discovery-level, would move only if the record showed her priority to be weaker than credited, and notes that B007 is so far ahead that the credit allocation may not be tested hard enough.
responses.response: His last concern is the right one: unanimity on rank should not substitute for testing the allocation, which is why I have tried to state the principle and not rely on the count. I agree that a contested priority in one direction is no better than one in the other. Where I partly differ is on B041, as I did not move on his two-person June and Sadelain pair: I find it defensible in itself, but the Eshhar and Gross originator question is outside the supplied credit and unresolved, which is why I keep B041 as the second alternative and not as a second part.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for identifying the active GLP-1(7-36) form is strong enough relative to Habener and others, which I cannot test from the supplied record.
Whether the committee adopts a discovery-level principle (Mojsov) or a development-inclusive one (Knudsen) for the third name.
Whether a two-part prize is feasible: B007 needs all three names, so any second part would require taking people from B007 or exceeding the cap.
How far the long-term safety and durability of obesity treatment should shape the wording of the citation.
statement.conflict_note: From my profile: I co-authored a 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons and a 2019 Physiological Reviews synthesis with Sten Grillner. I also use optogenetics (B032) as a research tool, and I did not place it in my configuration or alternatives. None of these involves a credited person on B007, B004 or B041, I have no documented personal tie to any credited name, and no recusal is needed. Nothing in round 1 changes this disclosure.
